title: Understanding Anxiety: When Everyday Worry Becomes a Struggle
excerpt: Anxiety is one of the most common mental health experiences — but there's a real difference between everyday stress and something that needs support. Here's how to tell them apart.
author: Dr. Ritu Sen
imageAlt: A person sitting quietly by a window, taking a calm breath
content: Almost everyone feels anxious sometimes — before an exam, a big conversation, or a change in life. That kind of worry is normal, and it usually passes once the moment does. Anxiety becomes something else when it lingers, shows up without a clear trigger, or starts shaping the choices you make each day.

Clinically, anxiety can look like a racing heart, tight chest, trouble sleeping, or a mind that won't stop rehearsing worst-case scenarios. It can also be quieter than that: a constant low hum of unease, a reluctance to commit to plans, or exhaustion that doesn't match how little you've actually done.

The most useful question isn't 'am I anxious' — almost everyone is, at some point — but 'is this anxiety getting in the way of my life.' If worry is costing you sleep, relationships, or the ability to do things you used to enjoy, that's the signal to reach out rather than wait it out.

Support for anxiety isn't one-size-fits-all. For some people it's talk therapy and learning to recognize thought patterns before they spiral. For others it includes breathing and grounding techniques, lifestyle changes, or medication alongside counseling. A good clinician will help you figure out what combination actually fits your life.

If any of this sounds familiar, you don't need a crisis to justify asking for help. Early support is often the difference between a hard season and a long one — and at Asha Foundation, that conversation can start whenever you're ready for it.
